quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Reduced Relative Clause with -ing
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence CANNOT be reduced to a simple participle phrase, unlike clauses with 'who' or 'which'?
quests.targetClause: The town where my grandmother was born has hardly changed.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence CANNOT be reduced to a simple participle phrase, unlike clauses with 'who' or 'which'?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Where' clauses show place, not a subject performing or receiving an action, so they don't reduce to a participle phrase the way 'who' or 'which' subject clauses do.
quests.nativeTip: Reduction works by dropping a subject relative pronoun and a form of 'be' - does 'where' introduce that same kind of clause?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The town where my grandmother was born has hardly changed."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Reduced Relative Clause with -ing
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence CANNOT be reduced to a participle phrase?
quests.targetClause: The year when the company was founded is engraved on the plaque.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence CANNOT be reduced to a participle phrase?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'When' clauses show time, not a subject performing or receiving an action, so, like 'where' clauses, they resist this kind of reduction.
quests.nativeTip: Ask whether the clause shows a time, or a subject doing or receiving an action.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The year when the company was founded is engraved on the plaque."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Reduced Relative Clause with -ing
quests.questionSentence: Which of these relative clause types CAN be reduced to a participle phrase?
quests.targetClause: Subject relative clauses with 'who,' 'which,' or 'that'
quests.completedSentence: Which of these relative clause types CAN be reduced to a participle phrase?
quests.ruleExplanation: Only subject relative clauses introduced by 'who,' 'which,' or 'that' reduce to a participle phrase; clauses with 'where,' 'when,' 'whose,' and object relative clauses generally cannot.
quests.nativeTip: Think back across everything covered so far in this phase - which single category of clause has consistently allowed reduction?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "Subject relative clauses with 'who,' 'which,' or 'that'"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Reduced Passive Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: The house that is being renovated will sell for more. Which is the correctly reduced form?
quests.targetClause: The house being renovated will sell for more.
quests.completedSentence: The house that is being renovated will sell for more. Which is the correctly reduced form?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Being renovated' keeps both the passive voice and the ongoing sense of 'that is being renovated'; simply saying 'renovated' would suggest the work is already finished.
quests.nativeTip: The original clause shows an action in progress and passive - which reduced form keeps both of those meanings?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The house being renovated will sell for more."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Reduced Passive Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: Compare: A) 'The proposal being reviewed by the board...' B) 'The proposal reviewed by the board...' Which one means the review is STILL happening right now?
quests.targetClause: Sentence A
quests.completedSentence: Compare: A) 'The proposal being reviewed by the board...' B) 'The proposal reviewed by the board...' Which one means the review is STILL happening right now?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Being reviewed' shows the review is currently in progress. 'Reviewed' alone suggests the review has already been completed.
quests.nativeTip: One version keeps the sense of an action in progress; the other suggests the action is already finished.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "Sentence A"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Reduced Passive Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: The patients ___ treated in the emergency room require immediate attention.
quests.targetClause: being
quests.completedSentence: The patients being treated in the emergency room require immediate attention.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Being treated' reduces 'who are being treated,' correctly keeping the ongoing, passive meaning.
quests.nativeTip: This describes patients currently undergoing treatment, in a passive and ongoing sense - which word captures both?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "being"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Reduced Passive Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: 'The horse raced past the barn fell.' Why does this sentence feel confusing on a first read?
quests.targetClause: 'Raced' looks like the main verb at first, but it's actually a reduced passive clause modifying 'horse,' and 'fell' is the real main verb.
quests.completedSentence: 'The horse raced past the barn fell.' Why does this sentence feel confusing on a first read?
quests.ruleExplanation: This is a classic 'garden path' sentence: readers first interpret 'raced' as the main verb, then hit 'fell' and must backtrack to realize 'raced past the barn' is a reduced passive clause describing which horse fell.
quests.nativeTip: Try reading it as: 'The horse [that was] raced past the barn fell.' Does that help it make more sense?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "'Raced' looks like the main verb at first, but it's actually a reduced passive clause modifying 'horse,' and 'fell' is the real main verb."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Reduced Passive Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: 'The suspect questioned by police confessed.' What is 'questioned by police' doing in this sentence?
quests.targetClause: It's a reduced passive clause describing 'the suspect' - the suspect was questioned by police.
quests.completedSentence: 'The suspect questioned by police confessed.' What is 'questioned by police' doing in this sentence?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Questioned by police' is a reduced passive clause modifying 'the suspect'; the real main verb is 'confessed.'
quests.nativeTip: Ask who questioned whom - did the suspect do the questioning, or receive it?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "It's a reduced passive clause describing 'the suspect' - the suspect was questioned by police."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Reduced Passive Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: Which rewrite avoids the initial confusion of 'The results collected during the trial surprised the researchers,' while keeping the same meaning?
quests.targetClause: The results that were collected during the trial surprised the researchers.
quests.completedSentence: Which rewrite avoids the initial confusion of 'The results collected during the trial surprised the researchers,' while keeping the same meaning?
quests.ruleExplanation: Restoring the full clause 'that were collected during the trial' removes any chance of misreading 'collected' as the main verb.
quests.nativeTip: The original could be briefly misread as 'the results collected the trial' before 'surprised' arrives - which rewrite removes that momentary confusion most simply?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The results that were collected during the trial surprised the researchers."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Reduced Passive Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: The report prepared by the analyst and reviewed by two directors was finally approved. How many reduced clauses does this sentence contain?
quests.targetClause: Two
quests.completedSentence: The report prepared by the analyst and reviewed by two directors was finally approved. How many reduced clauses does this sentence contain?
quests.ruleExplanation: There are two reduced clauses joined by 'and': 'prepared by the analyst' and 'reviewed by two directors,' both describing 'the report.'
quests.nativeTip: Look for each participle that could expand back into 'that was ___' - count them separately.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "Two"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Reduced Passive Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: Expand fully: 'The employees hired last year and trained by senior staff outperformed expectations.'
quests.targetClause: The employees who were hired last year and who were trained by senior staff outperformed expectations.
quests.completedSentence: Expand fully: 'The employees hired last year and trained by senior staff outperformed expectations.'
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Hired' and 'trained' are both past participles showing passive meaning, so both expand to 'who were': 'who were hired ... and who were trained ...'
quests.nativeTip: Both participles are passive - check that the expanded version uses the passive voice for each.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The employees who were hired last year and who were trained by senior staff outperformed expectations."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Reduced Relative Clause with -ing
quests.questionSentence: The team leading the project and impressed by the results celebrated together. What might feel slightly unusual about this sentence, and why?
quests.targetClause: It mixes an active reduction ('leading') with a passive one ('impressed'), which is grammatical but can feel stylistically unbalanced.
quests.completedSentence: The team leading the project and impressed by the results celebrated together. What might feel slightly unusual about this sentence, and why?
quests.ruleExplanation: The team actively leads the project ('leading') but passively receives the impression from the results ('impressed by the results') - both meanings are logically correct, even though mixing voices in one sentence can feel stylistically a little busy.
quests.nativeTip: Check whether the team is doing the leading (active) and doing or receiving the impressing (passive) - are both readings logically correct here?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "It mixes an active reduction ('leading') with a passive one ('impressed'), which is grammatical but can feel stylistically unbalanced."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Reduced Passive Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence correctly describes an email that SOMEONE ELSE is currently drafting?
quests.targetClause: The email being drafted by my assistant needs your approval before noon.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence correctly describes an email that SOMEONE ELSE is currently drafting?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Being drafted' correctly shows the passive, ongoing relationship: my assistant is currently drafting the email.
quests.nativeTip: The email isn't drafting itself - someone else is drafting it, and the action is ongoing. Which participle shows both?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The email being drafted by my assistant needs your approval before noon."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Reduced Relative Clause with -ing
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence correctly combines these facts: 'The satellite was launched in 2019. The satellite's data has transformed weather forecasting.'
quests.targetClause: The satellite, whose data has transformed weather forecasting, was launched in 2019.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence correctly combines these facts: 'The satellite was launched in 2019. The satellite's data has transformed weather forecasting.'
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Whose data has transformed weather forecasting' correctly keeps the possessive clause intact, since 'whose' clauses cannot be reduced to a participle phrase.
quests.nativeTip: The 'whose' clause must stay in full and unreduced; only check whether the rest of the sentence is grammatical.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The satellite, whose data has transformed weather forecasting, was launched in 2019."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Reduced Relative Clause with -ing
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence is grammatically flawed?
quests.targetClause: The manager, who overseeing three departments, rarely takes a lunch break.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence is grammatically flawed?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Who overseeing' incorrectly combines a relative pronoun with a reduced participle; it should read either 'who oversees three departments' or simply 'overseeing three departments,' never both together.
quests.nativeTip: A reduced clause never keeps its relative pronoun - check whether any option has accidentally kept one alongside a participle.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "The manager, who overseeing three departments, rarely takes a lunch break."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Possessive Relative Pronoun whose
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence contains a pronoun error?
quests.targetClause: The company which employees voted for new benefits announced the change.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence contains a pronoun error?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Which employees voted' incorrectly uses 'which' where possession is intended; the employees belong to the company, so 'whose employees voted' is correct.
quests.nativeTip: Check whether each pronoun matches its grammatical job - subject, object, or possession.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The company which employees voted for new benefits announced the change."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Object Relative Clause with which
quests.questionSentence: Which of these sentences misuses a relative pronoun?
quests.targetClause: The proposal whom the board rejected needs revision.
quests.completedSentence: Which of these sentences misuses a relative pronoun?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Whom the board rejected' should refer to a person, but here it wrongly refers to 'the proposal,' a thing; 'which the board rejected' is correct.
quests.nativeTip: Check whether the object pronoun in each sentence matches a person or a thing.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The proposal whom the board rejected needs revision."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Whom in Formal Register
quests.questionSentence: In a formal legal filing, which sentence contains a pronoun error?
quests.targetClause: The plaintiff who the court found liable has filed an appeal.
quests.completedSentence: In a formal legal filing, which sentence contains a pronoun error?
quests.ruleExplanation: In formal legal writing, an object pronoun for a person should be 'whom,' not 'who': 'the court found the plaintiff liable,' so 'the plaintiff' is the object and needs 'whom.'
quests.nativeTip: This is a formal legal document - check each object pronoun against the stricter, formal standard.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The plaintiff who the court found liable has filed an appeal."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted
quests.grammarRule: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence contains an omission error?
quests.targetClause: The employee missed the deadline apologized to the team.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence contains an omission error?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Missed the deadline' has no subject of its own - 'the employee' must supply it, so the relative pronoun cannot be dropped; it should read 'who missed the deadline.'
quests.nativeTip: Check whether each clause that needs its own subject actually has one.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The employee missed the deadline apologized to the team."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Non-Defining Clauses Cannot Omit Their Pronoun
quests.grammarRule: Non-Defining Clauses Cannot Omit Their Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence has wrongly dropped its relative pronoun?
quests.targetClause: This contract, we finally signed, took months to negotiate.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence has wrongly dropped its relative pronoun?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'This contract, we finally signed' drops the pronoun inside a non-defining clause, which is never allowed; it should read 'which we finally signed.'
quests.nativeTip: Check each clause set off by commas - does it still have a visible connecting word?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "This contract, we finally signed, took months to negotiate."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: No Relative Clause Needed (Hypercorrection)
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence contains an error involving an unnecessary relative pronoun?
quests.targetClause: I finally fixed that the leak yesterday.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence contains an error involving an unnecessary relative pronoun?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'I finally fixed that the leak yesterday' incorrectly inserts 'that' into what should be a simple sentence with no relative clause at all.
quests.nativeTip: Look for a sentence where a word like 'that' has been inserted even though nothing in the sentence needs a describing clause.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "I finally fixed that the leak yesterday."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Relative Adverb of Reason (why)
quests.questionSentence: Which of these sentences has a mistake?
quests.targetClause: The reason where she left the company was never explained.
quests.completedSentence: Which of these sentences has a mistake?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The reason where she left' incorrectly pairs 'where' with 'the reason'; it should be 'the reason why she left,' since 'why' is the relative adverb of reason.
quests.nativeTip: Match each relative word to its antecedent's category - is it a place, a time, a reason, or a person?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The reason where she left the company was never explained."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Relative Adverbs Cannot Be Subjects
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence below is not grammatical?
quests.targetClause: The delay why frustrated every passenger was never explained.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence below is not grammatical?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Why frustrated every passenger' incorrectly uses 'why' as the subject of 'frustrated'; relative adverbs can never serve as a clause's subject.
quests.nativeTip: Ask whether any relative adverb here is being forced to act as the subject of its own clause - something adverbs can never do.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The delay why frustrated every passenger was never explained."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Where vs Which/That for Places
quests.questionSentence: One of these sentences breaks a grammar rule - which one?
quests.targetClause: The venue where the company selected for the gala impressed every guest.
quests.completedSentence: One of these sentences breaks a grammar rule - which one?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Selected' takes 'the venue' as its direct object - the company selected the venue itself, not a location - so 'which' is needed, not 'where.'
quests.nativeTip: Check what the verb inside the clause needs - a location to happen in, or a direct object to receive the action.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The venue where the company selected for the gala impressed every guest."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Comma Placement in Non-Defining Clauses
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence contains a punctuation error, given that the speaker has only one sister?
quests.targetClause: My sister who lives in Berlin is visiting next month.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence contains a punctuation error, given that the speaker has only one sister?
quests.ruleExplanation: Since there is only one sister, 'who lives in Berlin' is non-defining and needs commas on both sides; without them, the sentence wrongly implies the speaker has several sisters.
quests.nativeTip: One sister means this clause is extra information - check the commas.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "My sister who lives in Berlin is visiting next month."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: That Cannot Introduce Non-Defining Clauses
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence contains a punctuation error?
quests.targetClause: The Amazon River, that is the largest river by discharge volume, flows through Brazil.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence contains a punctuation error?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'That' can never introduce a non-defining clause; since the Amazon River is unique, this clause needs 'which,' not 'that.'
quests.nativeTip: Check which relative pronoun is never allowed to follow a comma.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "The Amazon River, that is the largest river by discharge volume, flows through Brazil."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: A safety notice says: 'Workers, who operate heavy machinery, must wear ear protection.' Why is this punctuation likely a mistake?
quests.targetClause: The commas make the clause non-defining, incorrectly implying that all workers operate heavy machinery.
quests.completedSentence: A safety notice says: 'Workers, who operate heavy machinery, must wear ear protection.' Why is this punctuation likely a mistake?
quests.ruleExplanation: The commas turn the clause into extra, non-defining information, wrongly implying every worker operates heavy machinery. Without commas, the clause would correctly limit the rule to workers who operate such machinery.
quests.nativeTip: Think about who the notice is actually meant to apply to - all workers, or only some of them.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "The commas make the clause non-defining, incorrectly implying that all workers operate heavy machinery."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Preposition + whom/which (Fronted Preposition)
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence contains a preposition error?
quests.targetClause: The colleague with who I share an office is retiring.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence contains a preposition error?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Who' can never follow a preposition; after 'with,' a person requires 'whom': 'with whom I share an office.'
quests.nativeTip: Check which relative pronoun is allowed to follow a preposition directly.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The colleague with who I share an office is retiring."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Stranded Preposition in Relative Clauses
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence here is not correctly formed?
quests.targetClause: The house in which we grew up in was sold last year.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence here is not correctly formed?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'In which we grew up in' uses the preposition twice, once fronted and once stranded; only one of the two positions should be used.
quests.nativeTip: Count how many times the preposition appears - it should belong in only one place.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The house in which we grew up in was sold last year."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence is completely free of errors?
quests.targetClause: The advisor who guided my thesis, whom I met with regularly, has retired.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence is completely free of errors?
quests.ruleExplanation: This option correctly uses a defining clause ('who guided my thesis') to identify the advisor, followed by a non-defining clause ('whom I met with regularly') adding extra detail, with punctuation and pronouns both correct throughout.
quests.nativeTip: Check pronoun choice, comma placement, and whether any clause structure has been doubled or broken across all four options.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The advisor who guided my thesis, whom I met with regularly, has retired."
